result: The salivary gland placode in Drosophila is a flat, nearly circular epithelial primordium with an asymmetrically positioned invagination pit in the dorsal-posterior corner. Early apical constriction and cell wedging at this eccentric pit initiates tissue bending, with isotropic constriction driven by apical-medial actomyosin concentrated near the pit, while cell intercalation driven by polarised junctional actomyosin dominates at a distance from the pit.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are explicitly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A and related panels. The asymmetric positioning of the invagination pit and the spatial patterning of cell behaviors (apical constriction near the pit vs. intercalation far from the pit) are clearly documented with both textual descriptions and visual evidence. These claims are also supported by citations to previous work (Booth et al., 2014; Sanchez-Corrales et al., 2018), providing additional validation.

result: Cells near the invagination pit continuously constrict until internalized by approximately t=+20 min, while cells initially positioned far from the pit do not constrict significantly until t≈20 min when they move closer to the pit. Once in close proximity to the pit, these distant cells switch to apical constriction behavior, suggesting that cell behavior depends on position relative to the invagination point.
evaluation: Claims C6-C8 and C25-C29 are directly stated in the text and supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 1B-E. The temporal dynamics of apical area change for cells at different positions are clearly documented with time-lapse imaging and quantitative analysis. The interpretation that cells change behavior depending on their position relative to the pit (C27) is a reasonable inference from the presented data showing differential timing of constriction onset.

result: Apical constriction is always strongest near the invagination pit at any moment in time. As coronae of cells approach the pit region, they switch from predominantly intercalating to predominantly apically constricting/wedging. This continued near-pit constriction is driven by apical-medial myosin whose peak intensity and pulsatile strength tracks in a fixed position close to the pit over time, representing a dynamic adjustment of initially pre-patterned behavior.
evaluation: Claims C16-C18 and C32 are stated as findings from the study and supported by data in Figures 1 and 2. The spatial and temporal patterns of apical constriction and myosin activity are quantitatively documented. The interpretation of dynamic adjustment of pre-patterned behavior (C32) is a reasonable synthesis of the observed data showing position-dependent cell behavior changes over time.

result: Cells far from the pit initially show predominantly cell intercalation behavior that constricts the tissue primordium circumferentially whilst expanding it radially, thereby moving cells closer to the invagination pit.
evaluation: Claims C30-C31 are directly stated in the text, supported by Figure 1G, and cite previous work (Sanchez-Corrales et al., 2018). The description of intercalation behavior and its effect on tissue geometry is consistent with the strain rate analysis presented later in the manuscript (Figure 4).

result: Early apical constriction at the pit is driven by a highly dynamic apical-medial actomyosin network. Cells near the future invagination point at t=0 min show strong accumulation of apical-medial myosin, while cells far from the pit show mainly junctional myosin II accumulation. At t=30 min, cells that moved closer to the pit started to display apical-medial actomyosin, suggesting that being moved into a position near the invagination pit determines levels of apical-medial myosin accumulation.
evaluation: Claims C33-C38 are directly stated and supported by Figure 2A-B'' and citations to previous work. The spatial and temporal patterns of myosin accumulation are clearly documented with live imaging data. The interpretation that position near the pit determines myosin accumulation levels (C38) is a reasonable inference from the observed correlation between cell position and myosin levels.

result: The peak of apical-medial myosin fluorescence intensity and the location of shortest myosin II cycle lengths track in a near-fixed position to the edge of the pit over time. Cells near the pit at t=0 min show shorter myosin II cycle lengths and higher myosin strength compared to cells far from the pit. However, cells originally far from the pit increase their myosin strength over time as they move closer to the pit. This early asymmetric setup of high apical-medial myosin II intensity and activity near the pit is maintained during continued invagination, driving continued apical constriction near the pit.
evaluation: Claims C39-C46 are directly stated and supported by quantitative data in Figures 2D-H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The spatial and temporal patterns of myosin intensity, cycle length, and strength are quantitatively documented. Statistical significance is reported (p<0.0001, Mann Whitney test) for differences between near and far pit cells. The correlation between longer cycle length and unproductive myosin cycles (C42) is supported by citation to previous work (Booth et al., 2014).

result: In hkb−/− mutants, a central invagination pit forms with significant delay compared to the eccentric pit in wild-type placodes, and the overall morphogenesis is disrupted with malformed invaginated salivary glands at later stages. At t~+40 min, no invagination had occurred in hkb−/− mutants whereas most secretory cells had already invaginated in wild-type embryos. Eventually, hkb−/− mutant embryos invaginate a dilated tube through an enlarged pit.
evaluation: Claims C9, C47-C50, C53, and C62 are directly stated and supported by Figures 3A'''-F''' and Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The phenotypic differences between wild-type and hkb−/− mutants are clearly documented with both live imaging and fixed samples. Claims C9, C47, and C48 also cite previous work (Myat and Andrew, 2000b; 2002), providing additional validation of the mutant phenotype.

result: In wild-type placodes, the area of strongest apical area constriction is always located near the pit. In contrast, in hkb−/− mutant placodes, cells begin to constrict in an aberrant central position from about t=+20-30 min. Cells near the central pit in hkb−/− mutants start to constrict at a much slower rate than wild-type cells near the eccentric pit, and only from about t=+20 min onwards. The rate of constriction of central cells in hkb−/− mutants is very similar to that of cells located at a distance to the pit in wild-type, suggesting that central cells in hkb−/− mutants behave identically to wild-type cells occupying the same position.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 and C54-C58 are directly stated and supported by quantitative data in Figures 3G-J. The spatial and temporal patterns of apical area constriction are quantitatively documented for both wild-type and hkb−/− mutants. The comparison of constriction rates between different cell populations (C55-C56) is supported by the data shown in Figure 3J, though the interpretation that cells behave according to their position (C56) is an inference that could benefit from additional statistical testing.

result: hkb−/− mutant placodes show no accumulation of apical-medial actomyosin at the eccentric position where a pit forms in wild-type. Instead, only at t~+40 min does a central group of cells display increased accumulation of apical-medial myosin II, inducing shallow tissue bending in this region. These analyses strongly suggest that the initial asymmetrical setup of cell behaviors in the placode is disrupted in hkb−/− embryos.
evaluation: Claims C59-C61 and C63 are directly stated and supported by Figures 3E, 3K, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, with comparison to wild-type data in Figure 2D. The spatial and temporal patterns of myosin accumulation in hkb−/− mutants are clearly documented. The interpretation that the asymmetrical setup is disrupted (C63) is a reasonable inference from the observed shift from eccentric to central myosin accumulation.

result: Strain rate analysis reveals distinct patterns in wild-type versus hkb−/− mutants. In wild-type, cells near the eccentric pit constrict isotropically with near equal tissue and cell shape strain and minimal intercalation, while cells far from the pit show intercalations leading to circumferential convergence and radial extension, then switch to apical contraction after t=+20 min once closer to the pit. In hkb−/− mutants, cells near the central pit show much reduced tissue and cell shape strain rates with constriction commencing at about half the rate of wild-type from t=+20 min onwards. Cells far from the central pit in hkb−/− mutants show slight tissue expansion in both directions with cell shapes narrowing radially and extending circumferentially.
evaluation: Claims C64-C72 are directly stated and supported by quantitative strain rate analysis in Figures 4A-B'' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The strain rate analysis is based on established methods (Blanchard et al., 2009) and provides detailed quantification of tissue deformation, cell shape changes, and intercalation. Statistical significance is determined using mixed-effects models (p<0.05), as indicated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The data clearly show the differences between wild-type and hkb−/− mutants in both spatial patterns and temporal dynamics of strain rates.

result: Analysis of neighbor gains reveals that in wild-type placodes, circumferential neighbor gains dominate over radial ones throughout, leading to steady increase in cumulative productive neighbor gains. In contrast, in hkb−/− mutant embryos, circumferential and radial neighbor gains are overall much reduced and occur with equal frequency. Cells near the delayed central pit in hkb−/− mutants show no productive neighbor gains, while cells at the periphery show productive neighbor gains. Active neighbor gains are initiated and driven by junctional actomyosin, and in control placodes junctional myosin is clearly enriched in circumferential junctions, while in hkb−/− mutant placodes myosin unipolarity and bipolarity are strongly reduced.
evaluation: Claims C73-C79 are directly stated and supported by quantitative analysis in Figures 4C-G. The neighbor gain analysis is clearly defined and quantified, with data pooled from multiple movies (nine wild-type and five hkb−/− mutant movies as stated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Statistical significance is indicated in Figure 4F-G using mixed-effects models (p<0.05, p<0.005, p<0.0005). The connection between junctional actomyosin and neighbor gains (C77) is supported by citations to previous work (Sanchez-Corrales et al., 2018; Tetley et al., 2016).

result: Cell elongation analysis shows that in wild-type placodes, cells far from the pit are initially elongated circumferentially at t<+20 min during early intercalation, then become increasingly elongated radially as they move nearer to the pit. In hkb−/− mutant embryos, cells far from the pit quickly become circumferentially elongated and remain so throughout. Although cells far from the central pit in hkb−/− mutants still intercalate and gain circumferential neighbors, this behavior lacks several key signatures of wild-type intercalations, and overall intercalations do not lead to convergence and extension toward the misplaced pit. These analyses show that in the absence of Hkb, the initial radial patterning of cell behaviors across the placode is highly aberrant, and cells at the position corresponding to the wild-type eccentric pit clearly fail to constrict apically, suggesting Hkb could be involved in specification of this pit behavior.
evaluation: Claims C80-C87 are directly stated and supported by data in Figure 4H and analysis of individual intercalation events in Figure 4I-L. The cell elongation analysis is quantified and shows clear differences between wild-type and hkb−/− mutants. The interpretation that intercalations lack key signatures of wild-type behavior (C83-C84) is supported by the observation that intercalations do not lead to tissue convergence and extension in mutants. The conclusion that Hkb is involved in pit specification (C87) is stated as a suggestion/speculation based on the data, which is appropriate given the correlative nature of the evidence.

result: Using endogenously tagged Venus-Hkb, the authors detected Hkb at high levels concentrated in the dorsal-posterior region of the forming placode at t=−30 min prior to tissue bending, and as early as t=−63 min prior to invagination. Venus-Hkb expression then expanded more broadly and anteriorly across the whole placode over time. At t=0 min, Venus-Hkb was found across the placode with elevated levels at the invagination pit position and a second increase toward the anterior. At late stages (t>>0 min), Venus-Hkb levels close to the invagination point were lower than further anterior. Thus, Hkb shows a clear temporally and spatially graded pattern of expression within the early placode that develops dynamically, with changes especially pronounced at the dorsal-posterior corner with highest levels already an hour before tissue bending commenced.
evaluation: Claims C88-C92, C97-C98 are directly stated and supported by live imaging and quantification in Figures 5A-F, 5M, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B''. The Venus-Hkb reporter was generated using CRISPR/Cas9 to tag the endogenous protein, providing confidence that the observed pattern reflects endogenous Hkb expression. The quantification in Figure 5M pools data from time-lapse movies and fixed samples with specified cell numbers (n=777-1186 cells from 8-10 embryos at different stages), providing statistical robustness.

result: Using an in vivo genomic GFP-Fkh reporter, Fkh-GFP was visible in cells near the future invagination pit at t=−60 min prior to tissue bending, from where it spread anteriorly and ventrally across the whole placode. At t=0 min, Fkh-GFP was detected in all cells of the placode with levels still highest near the pit and decreasing toward the anterior edge. At t=+30 min and beyond, levels of Fkh-GFP were more uniform across the placode.
evaluation: Claims C93-C96 are directly stated and supported by live imaging and quantification in Figures 5G-L, 5N, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-C''. The Fkh-GFP reporter is from an established source (Bloomington BDSC:43951) and the observed pattern is validated by comparison with anti-Fkh antibody staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-C''). The quantification in Figure 5N pools data from time-lapse movies and fixed samples with specified cell numbers (n=365-1026 cells from 4-9 embryos at different stages).

result: Combined Hkb and Fkh action could define the future position of the invagination pit. Venus-Hkb intensity levels peaked in cells at the site of the forming eccentric invagination pit at about t~−30 min, with appearance of smaller apical areas following about 30-40 min later. Similarly, Fkh-GFP intensity began to peak at about t~−30 min and then tracked at high level at a fixed distance to the pit over time, with increased reduction in apical area appearing with a delay of about 30-40 min. Such a delay would be consistent with the estimated time required for transcription, translation, protein folding, secretion, binding to receptor, and signaling leading to myosin phosphorylation. Thus, Hkb and Fkh dynamic expression at the future eccentric pit could prefigure the start of apical constriction at this site, and the continuous high levels of Fkh tracking at a fixed distance to the pit suggest that Fkh is key to the continuous apical constriction of cells moving into a near pit position.
evaluation: Claims C99-C106 are directly stated and supported by data in Figures 5O-P'. The temporal correlation between transcription factor expression peaks and subsequent apical area reduction is clearly documented. The 30-40 min delay (C101, C103) is consistent with the time required for the molecular cascade from transcription to myosin activation (C104), as supported by citations (Garcia et al., 2013; Shamir et al., 2016). The interpretations that Hkb/Fkh expression prefigures apical constriction (C105) and that Fkh is key to continuous constriction (C106) are reasonable inferences from the temporal and spatial correlations observed.

result: Dynamic changes in Hkb and Fkh expression might trigger the graded and patterned expression of targets of both transcription factors, leading to the observed patterned cell behaviors and the switch between intercalation and constriction.
evaluation: Claim C107 is explicitly stated as speculation ('might trigger') based on the observed correlations between transcription factor expression patterns and cell behaviors. While the temporal and spatial correlations are well-documented, direct evidence that Hkb and Fkh trigger downstream target expression in a graded manner is not provided. This would require additional experiments such as measuring downstream target expression levels or manipulating Hkb/Fkh levels to test causality.

result: Previous studies have shown that several proteins including the transcription factor Forkhead (Fkh), the dynein-associated protein Klar, and the kinase Btk29 are initially expressed in the dorsal posterior region of the placode. In agreement with this, fkh−/− mutants specifically fail to apically constrict in the dorsal-posterior corner, though they do show intercalation behavior, and these mutants do not invaginate a tube.
evaluation: Claims C10-C15 cite previous work (Myat and Andrew, 2000a, 2002; Chandrasekaran and Beckendorf, 2005; Sanchez-Corrales et al., 2018) and are consistent with the current study's findings. The fkh−/− mutant phenotype (C13-C15) is supported by both the cited previous work and data presented in this manuscript (e.g., Figure 6Q-T showing lack of Fog enrichment in fkh−/− mutants).

result: The GPCR-ligand Folded gastrulation (Fog) was found to be dependent on Fkh and suggested to be downstream of Hkb. Fog is an apically secreted ligand that acts in an autocrine fashion, and thus cells that switch on Fog expression will apically constrict. Previously published in situ hybridization of fog mRNA suggested increased levels near the forming pit, similar to the early Hkb and Fkh enrichment.
evaluation: Claims C108-C112 cite previous work (Chung et al., 2017; Dawes-Hoang et al., 2005; Myat and Andrew, 2000b; Nikolaidou and Barrett, 2004) and are consistent with the current study's findings. The dependence of Fog on Fkh (C108) is supported by data in Figure 6Q-T showing loss of Fog enrichment in fkh−/− mutants. The autocrine action of Fog (C110-C111) is established knowledge from cited work.

result: Fog expression and signaling could be upstream of the isotropic constriction of cells near the forming pit, and could also be involved in maintaining this behavior in new coronae of cells moving into a position near the pit over time.
evaluation: Claims C113-C114 are explicitly stated as speculation ('could be') in the text. While the spatial and temporal correlation between Fog expression and apical constriction is well-documented in this study (Figures 6A-L), direct causal evidence that Fog is upstream of constriction or maintains this behavior over time is not provided. The Fog overexpression experiments (Figure 7) provide some support for Fog's role in driving constriction, but do not directly test the maintenance hypothesis.

result: Fog levels were low at mid-stage 10 concomitant with placode specification. Just before tissue bending commenced at t=0 min, Fog was strongly enriched in cells near the forming invagination pit, and these cells were the ones already showing decreased apical area. Fog protein levels remained enriched near the invagination point once the tube had started to internalize. Fog protein levels in cells were positively correlated with both smaller apical areas and higher average apical-medial myosin II intensity.
evaluation: Claims C115-C120 are directly stated and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 6A-L and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The spatial and temporal patterns of Fog protein are clearly documented. The correlations between Fog levels and apical area (C119) and myosin intensity (C120) are quantified with Pearson coefficients (r=−0.436 and r=0.439 respectively, n=823 cells from seven embryos), providing statistical support for the relationships.

result: At late stage 11, Fog protein levels in hkb−/− mutant embryos appeared similar to wild-type and enriched in the placode compared to surrounding epidermis, though the pattern of Fog enrichment was altered. Cells at the posterior corner where the invagination pit would have formed in wild-type lacked high Fog protein levels, whereas only cells in the center of the placode showed high levels of Fog protein. Quantitative analysis showed the peak intensity of Fog protein in hkb−/− mutants was clearly shifted to a central, much more symmetrical, position.
evaluation: Claims C121-C125 are directly stated and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 6M-P. The altered pattern of Fog enrichment in hkb−/− mutants is clearly documented, with quantification from multiple embryos (n=765 cells from five embryos) showing the shift from eccentric to central Fog accumulation. This provides strong evidence for Hkb's role in patterning Fog expression.

result: In fkh−/− embryos at late stage 11, Fog protein was no longer enriched at the position where the invagination pit forms in wild-type, and Fog levels did not appear raised anywhere within the placode compared to the surrounding epidermis.
evaluation: Claims C126-C127 are directly stated and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 6Q-T and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-D''. The loss of Fog enrichment in fkh−/− mutants is clearly documented with quantification from multiple embryos (n=512 cells from five embryos), providing strong evidence for Fkh's role in regulating Fog expression.

result: In both hkb−/− and fkh−/− mutants, altered levels and patterning of Fog protein still correlated with the altered levels and patterns of residual apical-medial myosin. At late stage 10, the Fkh protein expression pattern in hkb−/− mutants was indistinguishable from control and remained identical to wild-type throughout stage 11 and beyond. The natural expansion of Fkh protein expression to cells in the center of the placode observed in hkb−/− mutant placodes might be the cause of the delayed constriction of cells in this region, whereas the earlier initial constriction at the site of the eccentric pit was absent in the mutant because it requires both Fkh and Hkb. Both transcription factors appeared to be independently regulated, as Hkb levels and protein expression pattern were unchanged in fkh−/− mutant embryos.
evaluation: Claims C128-C134 are directly stated and supported by data in Figures 6M, 6Q, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-N'. The correlation between Fog and myosin patterns in mutants (C128) is documented. The independence of Hkb and Fkh regulation (C133-C134) is supported by showing that each transcription factor's expression pattern is unaffected in the other's mutant background. The interpretation that both factors are required for early eccentric pit constriction (C132) is a reasonable inference from the mutant phenotypes, though the causal mechanism is not directly tested.

result: The asymmetrical setup of the salivary gland placode prior to initiation of tube budding relies on correct spatial and temporal patterning of the key transcription factors Hkb and Fkh. These transcription factors are upstream of GPCR/Fog signaling that leads to patterned and sustained apical-medial myosin activity and contractile cell behaviors. The asymmetrical invagination point depends on patterning by transcription factors and downstream GPCRs/Fog signaling at the posterior corner, leading to a focussed and point-like invagination pit.
evaluation: Claims C135-C137 are stated as conclusions from the data and supported by the comprehensive analysis of transcription factor expression patterns (Figures 5), Fog expression patterns (Figure 6), and mutant phenotypes (Figures 3-4, 6). The hierarchical relationship (Hkb/Fkh → Fog → myosin → cell behaviors) is supported by the temporal correlations, spatial patterns, and mutant analyses. Claim C137 also cites previous work (Chung et al., 2017; Myat and Andrew, 2000a, 2000b, 2002; Sanchez-Corrales et al., 2018) for additional support.

result: Overexpression of Fog in the salivary gland placode using UAS-Fog x fkhGal4 led to placode-wide increased levels of Fog from early stages on. When Fog was overexpressed, most secretory cells of the placode constricted simultaneously at early stage 11, forming a large shallow depression across the whole dorsal part of the placode at late stage 11. At stage 12, this whole section formed a deepened very wide pit. The widened tube in Fog-overexpressing embryos at stages 15-16 displayed a significantly enlarged and flattened lumen compared to wild-type tubes. Overexpression of Fkh using UAS-Fkh x fkhGal4 led to a similarly enlarged area of apical constriction early on and invaginated tubes with aberrant and inflated lumens at late stages.
evaluation: Claims C138-C143 are directly stated and supported by data in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplements 1-2. The Fog overexpression phenotype is clearly documented with both live imaging and fixed samples at multiple stages. Statistical significance of the lumen enlargement (C142) is reported (Mann-Whitney test, p<0.0001; wild-type n=23 embryos, UAS-Fog x fkhGal4 n=20 embryos). The similar phenotype with Fkh overexpression (C143) provides additional support for the Fkh→Fog pathway.

result: Theoretical considerations and experimental observations show that in wild-type, a focussed eccentric pit leads to similar numbers of cells invaginating within each corona. In contrast, a centrally located pit would lead to an ever-increasing number of cells per corona that would need to invaginate, and an enlarged pit would lead to invagination of a large number of cells initially, followed by similarly large numbers in each corona. The actual numbers of invaginating coronae of cells observed in wild-type, hkb−/−, and UAS-Fog x fkhGal4 embryos were in very good agreement with the theoretical considerations.
evaluation: Claims C144-C147 are directly stated and supported by theoretical modeling (Figures 7K-N) and experimental quantification (Figure 7O). The theoretical considerations are based on simple geometric principles, and the experimental data (n=30 wild-type, n=11 hkb−/−, n=5 UAS-Fog x fkhGal4 embryos) show good agreement with the predictions. This provides strong support for the functional importance of the eccentric pit position in controlling the number of invaginating cells per corona.

result: In hkb−/− mutant embryos, the delayed central area of constriction turned into a widened invagination and the enlarged pit at late stages often collapsed into an enlarged crescent of subduction at the boundary, leading to malformed and enlarged lumen glands. Thus, the eccentrically placed invagination pit in the dorsal-posterior corner of the salivary gland placode is a key factor in ensuring the formation of a symmetrical narrow lumen tube during invagination, in part likely due to the control over the number of invaginating cells in each corona destined to internalize.
evaluation: Claims C148-C150 are directly stated and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—videos 3-4, and the theoretical/experimental analysis in Figure 7. The malformed gland phenotype in hkb−/− mutants (C148) is documented and cites previous work (Myat and Andrew, 2002). The conclusion that the eccentric pit is key to symmetrical tube formation (C149-C150) is supported by the combination of mutant phenotypes, overexpression phenotypes, and the geometric analysis showing how pit position affects the number of invaginating cells.

result: A temporal and spatial component is provided by the dynamically changing pattern of the transcription factors Hkb and Fkh, which are expressed initially with the highest protein level at the point where the invagination pit will form, before expression expands further across the placode over time. This ensures that cells in the dorsal-posterior corner are the first to experience high levels of activity of these transcription factors, and one of the important targets, the GPCR-ligand Fog, is found at high levels in these cells in a Hkb- and Fkh-dependent manner with a slight temporal delay. As cells continuously internalize to form the tube, new coronae of cells are brought into a 'near the pit' position and adjust their behavior accordingly. This position-specific behavior of apical constriction is most likely triggered by the previous temporal expansion of Fkh and Hkb expression to these cells, thereby priming them for their next step in tube formation.
evaluation: Claims C151-C156 are stated as a summary of the findings and supported by the comprehensive data on transcription factor expression dynamics (Figure 5), Fog expression patterns (Figure 6), and cell behavior dynamics (Figures 1-2). The temporal and spatial correlations are well-documented. The interpretation that position-specific behavior is triggered by prior transcription factor expression (C156) is a reasonable inference from the observed temporal delays and spatial patterns, though direct causal testing would require additional experiments.

result: The pattern of Fkh and Hkb expression from t=0 min onwards is not identical, suggesting that downstream targets begin to diverge at later stages. The hkb−/− mutant analysis suggests that central cells in the placode that manage to constrict in the absence of Hkb might only require Fkh activity to initiate Fog expression and function. These cells undergo their normal apical constriction once Fkh expression has reached the central position, and as they are now the first cells to constrict and invaginate, hkb−/− mutants show a central and delayed constriction and invagination. This work strongly suggests that the combined early patterning of Hkb and Fkh expression defines the early invagination pit and its eccentric position.
evaluation: Claims C157-C161 are stated as interpretations of the data and supported by the differential expression patterns of Hkb and Fkh (Figure 5M-N), the hkb−/− mutant phenotype (Figures 3-4), and the Fkh expression pattern in hkb−/− mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-J'). The interpretation that central cells in hkb−/− mutants only require Fkh (C158-C159) is a reasonable inference from the observation that these cells eventually constrict when Fkh expression reaches them, though direct testing would require additional experiments. The conclusion that combined Hkb and Fkh patterning defines the eccentric pit (C161) is well-supported by the mutant phenotypes and expression patterns.

result: Both Hkb and Fkh are expressed in the placode downstream of the homeotic factor Sex Combs Reduced (Scr). At the time point when Hkb and Fkh expression at the future pit location commences, Wg expression within the placode region is confined to the dorsal-posterior corner only. Future studies will show whether a combination of Scr and Wg transcription factor activity could activate early pit-defining expression of factors such as Fkh and Hkb.
evaluation: Claims C162-C163 cite previous work (Myat and Andrew, 2000b; Panzer et al., 1992) for the Scr relationship and state unpublished observations for the Wg pattern. Claim C164 is explicitly stated as speculation about future work. While the upstream regulation of Hkb and Fkh is not directly tested in this study, the cited previous work provides support for the Scr relationship, and the Wg observation (though unpublished) is consistent with the spatial pattern of Hkb/Fkh expression.

result: In addition to transcription factors, some potential downstream effectors also appear to be expressed near the future pit location first, including Btk29/Tec29, Crumbs, 18-Wheeler, and Klarsicht.
evaluation: Claims C165-C168 cite previous work (Chandrasekaran and Beckendorf, 2005; Myat and Andrew, 2002; Röper, 2012; Kolesnikov and Beckendorf, 2007) for the expression patterns of these proteins. While these patterns are not directly examined in the current study, the cited previous work provides support for these claims.

result: Activation of actomyosin contractility through GPCR signaling driven by the autocrine secretion of the ligand Fog is a module repeatedly used during tissue bending and invagination events in Drosophila embryogenesis. What differs are the upstream activating transcription factors: during mesoderm invagination Fog expression on the ventral side is controlled by Twist and Snail, whereas its expression during posterior midgut invagination is controlled by Tailless and Hkb. The effect of Hkb on Fog expression is likely direct, as the Fog locus contains predicted Hkb-binding sites.
evaluation: Claims C169-C171 cite previous work (Morize et al., 1998; Weigel et al., 1990) and represent established knowledge about the Fog signaling module in different developmental contexts. Claim C172 is supported by computational prediction of Hkb-binding sites in the Fog locus using oPOSSUM, though direct experimental validation of Hkb binding to these sites is not provided. The prediction is consistent with the observed Hkb-dependence of Fog expression shown in this study.

result: The identity of the GPCR that could mediate the Fog signal in the salivary gland placode is unclear. Published and database in situs for the GPCRs Mist and Smog do not show enriched expression in the placode.
evaluation: Claims C173-C174 are directly stated and cite previous work (Kerridge et al., 2016; Manning et al., 2013) for the Mist and Smog expression patterns. The statement that the GPCR identity is unclear (C173) is an honest acknowledgment of a gap in current knowledge.

result: Recent work analyzing mesoderm invagination in Drosophila has shown that T48 and Fog show a gradient of expression due to differential timing of transcriptional activation, and flattening the gradient experimentally leads to a widened and perturbed invagination process. By contrast, the invagination of the posterior midgut does not require sustained transcription, but instead a wave of apical constriction appears to be propagated via mechanical feedback. The salivary gland placode seems to follow a model of a temporal expansion or wave of transcriptional activity translating into positionally fixed behaviors. Nonetheless, quantitative analysis of 3D cell behaviors strongly indicated that mechanical feedback does also play a role.
evaluation: Claims C175-C180 cite previous work (Lim et al., 2017; Heer et al., 2017; Bailles et al., 2019; Sanchez-Corrales et al., 2018) and provide context for the current findings. The comparison of different morphogenetic mechanisms (C175-C178) is supported by the cited work. The conclusion that the salivary gland placode follows a transcriptional wave model (C179) is a reasonable interpretation of the data presented in this study. The acknowledgment that mechanical feedback also plays a role (C180) cites previous work and is consistent with the current findings.

result: The posterior spiracle placode, like the salivary gland placode, is a flat epithelium with an eccentric invagination point.
evaluation: Claim C181 cites previous work (Sidor et al., 2020; Simões et al., 2006) and provides comparative context suggesting that the asymmetric placodal setup may be a conserved feature of tube formation processes. While this is not directly examined in the current study, the cited previous work provides support for this claim.
